\begin{figure}[H]
  \captionsetup{font=footnotesize}  % 10 pt caption (footnotesize at 12 pt base)
  \caption{\textbf{Patch-leaving behavior is consistent with a Bayesian formulation of the Marginal Value Theorem.}
    (\subref{fig:3-a}) MVT predicts that an optimal forager leaves a patch when the instantaneous marginal reward rate falls below the global average reward rate, set by travel time between patches and within-patch reward statistics.
    (\subref{fig:3-b}) Reward probability at leaving is matched across patch types (ns), while rewards collected and number of reward omissions experienced differed significantly, ruling out simple heuristics such as reward counting or win-stay/loose switch. Lines connect individual animals ($N=24$), Odor 1 (orange) and odor 2 (green) patch types.
    (\subref{fig:3-c}) Probability of leaving if the first odor site in a patch was unrewarded. Mice were more likely to leave the Low than the High patch after identical failure sequences, reflecting odor-cued prior expectations about patch quality.
    (\subref{fig:3-d}) Change in $P(\text{reward})$ at leaving relative to control as a function of inter-patch travel distance. Longer distances led mice to leave at lower reward probabilities, while shorter distances produced the opposite effect, consistent with MVT predictions.
    (\subref{fig:3-e}) Change in $P(\text{reward})$ at leaving relative to control as a function of inter-patch wheel friction. Increased friction raises the effective travel cost, leading mice to leave patches at lower reward probabilities.
    (\subref{fig:3-f},\subref{fig:3-h}) Reward probability depletion curves for the transition to a higher (\subref{fig:3-f}) and lower (\subref{fig:3-h}) global reward rate. In (\subref{fig:3-f}), odor 2 reward statistics were increased to match those of odor 1; in (\subref{fig:3-h}), odor 1 reward statistics were decreased to match those of odor 2. Solid lines show the new reward statistics; faded lines show the original conditions.
    (\subref{fig:3-g}) Change in $P(\text{reward})$ at leaving relative to control under increased global reward rate conditions in mice. Both patch types shifted to higher reward probabilities, meaning mice left patches earlier. To achieve this, rewards collected shifted in opposite directions across patch types. This demonstrates cross-patch generalization consistent with global reward rate integration.
    (\subref{fig:3-i}) Opposite to (\subref{fig:3-g}); under decreased global reward rate, both patch types shifted to lower reward probabilities, with rewards collected shifting in opposite directions across patch types.
    (\subref{fig:3-j}) Bayesian MVT model schematic. The agent maintains a separate posterior over reward probability $q$ for each odor-cued patch type, updated after each binary outcome via Bayes' rule with a forgetting parameter $\delta < 1$ that discounts accumulated prior beliefs at each update step. At each odor site, a sample $\tilde{q}$ is drawn from the current posterior; the agent leaves if the implied local reward rate falls below a running estimate of the global reward rate $\bar{R}$.
    (\subref{fig:3-k}--\subref{fig:3-n}) Bayesian MVT model simulations reproducing the mouse results in (\subref{fig:3-b}--\subref{fig:3-e}): reward probability at leaving and rewards collected (\subref{fig:3-k}), probability of leaving after early consecutive omissions (\subref{fig:3-l}), change in $P(\text{reward})$ at leaving with inter-patch distance (\subref{fig:3-m}), and inter-patch friction (\subref{fig:3-n}).
    (\subref{fig:3-o},\subref{fig:3-q}) Model simulation depletion curves for the transition to a higher (\subref{fig:3-o}) and lower (\subref{fig:3-q}) global reward rate, corresponding to (\subref{fig:3-f}) and (\subref{fig:3-h}).
    (\subref{fig:3-p},\subref{fig:3-r}) Same as (\subref{fig:3-g}) and (\subref{fig:3-i}) for Bayesian MVT model simulations, reproducing the cross-patch generalization observed in mice.
    Significance (paired $t$-tests across subjects): ns, not significant; $^{*}p<0.05$, $^{**}p<0.01$, $^{***}p<0.001$.}
  \label{fig:3}
\end{figure}
